Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

fall, the Lantern College Film Society is building a program around movies made in small towns and the way public places change when people move away. We have forty-three active members on the mailing list and twelve people who have volunteered for at least one shift. Our usual meetings are in the media lab on Tuesdays, but the lab is booked for a photography class on October 8, so we are meeting in the library seminar room that night. The room has a screen but no speakers, and Professor Elian said we can borrow the portable set from the language department if we return it before noon on Wednesday. We are keeping the program open to students and staff, and guests will need to sign in at the front desk.

The opening film is a fictional documentary called *The Mile Marker*, about a family-run diner beside a highway that was rerouted in 1986. The filmmaker has emailed a permission letter for one campus screening, and the society has to send the final date and room before the letter is complete. Our second choice is a comedy called *June at the Depot*, which follows two cousins trying to keep a town train station open as a community space. We have not heard back from that director yet, so it stays a backup rather than a confirmed title. Leah found a short film by an alum named Oren Vale that could fit before either feature, but it is only nine minutes and has captions in English and Spanish. She wants to ask whether the filmmaker would join us by video for a question period.

At Monday's planning meeting, we looked at the old poster template and agreed the society name should be bigger than the film titles because people kept reading the date but missing who was presenting. Niko was assigned the projection coordinator role, and Lale was assigned treasurer, so the equipment receipts go to Lale and the projector checklist goes to Niko. Our secretary, Imani, will update the shared calendar after we confirm the room. She has marked October 15 as a possible date for the first screening, not a final booking, because the student union has not sent its fall events list. She said, “I can hold the evening on our calendar, but I cannot promise the auditorium until the union checks for a conflict.”

The society has a small budget of six hundred and eighty dollars from its student activities allocation. Ninety dollars is already set aside for captioning two older films, and the print shop quoted one dollar and twenty cents per color poster if we order at least thirty. We have fourteen folding display stands in the equipment closet, although two have cracked feet and should not go near the stairwell. The library can lend us a table for the lobby, but we need to request it three business days ahead. Last spring, some guests waited outside the wrong entrance because our signs pointed toward the loading door, so this time we want one sign at the courtyard gate and another beside the accessible entrance.

We also want the program to feel welcoming to people who do not know much about film discussion. Jules suggested giving each guest a card with two questions, one about a detail they noticed and one about how the setting shaped the story. Dev said the cards should not ask people to explain what a film means, since that can sound like there is only one correct answer. At the last meeting, Mina brought a map of the neighborhood around the old Rialto cinema and showed where the bus stops moved after the street redesign. The map might be useful for the lobby display, but we need permission from the local history archive before we reproduce it. Mina has the archivist's email and plans to ask about a low-resolution copy for one evening.

1. Confirm the room and screening date with the student union and send the filmmaker the details.
2. Ask the language department about borrowing the speakers and write the return time on the equipment sheet.
3. Get an estimate from the print shop for thirty posters and check whether they can deliver them to the media lab.
4. Ask Oren Vale if he is available for a video question period and whether the short has a separate caption file.
5. Make a new projector checklist and put the contact number for campus support at the top.

Those are tasks for the committee before the next Tuesday meeting, and Imani said she can circulate the list on Monday morning.

If the weather service predicts heavy rain by noon on the screening day, we should move the courtyard welcome table inside the library entrance and ask two volunteers to guide people from the bus stop. If the forecast is clear, the table can stay by the courtyard gate, but we still need to keep the accessible entrance unobstructed. This condition matters because the library has only one indoor lobby table and another student group may reserve it. We should not print the welcome signs until the room is confirmed, so the location line does not have to be covered with tape.

At the next meeting, we will compare the available dates with the union calendar and decide whether *The Mile Marker* can be the opening film or whether *June at the Depot* should remain the first option. Nobody has chosen a final film yet. Lale will bring the budget sheet, and Niko will bring the projector checklist with the speaker cable lengths written down. The society can invite the history archive after we know whether the map may be displayed, and we can ask the filmmaker about a video visit once the date is firm. Imani wants to leave ten minutes at the end of the meeting for members to raise other ideas, including a possible spring workshop on making captions. She said we should write down questions even if we cannot answer them that night, so the next program does not depend on one person's memory."}]
